note: Words an accusation's rationale may not use, because each one asserts
something about a person — their intent, their honesty, or a conclusion
about their conduct — rather than describing grounding (the project rules,
rule 2). The rationale is the one string in this system written by a model
and shown to a person, so the restriction is enforced in code:
`backend/app/agents/loop.py` loads this list and refuses an `accuse` call
that matches it, naming the word, before the tool runs. The model is told
the same thing in its system prompt, but that only saves a turn; this file
is the guarantee.
THIS LIST IS DELIBERATELY WIDER THAN RULE 2. Rule 2 names four words; this
names twenty. The rest are the same assertion in other clothes, and a later
reader should not prune it back to four on the grounds that the rule only
lists four. Two are worth calling out. `fabricate` and `fabrication`
overlap with the referee's own DELIBERATE_FABRICATION label, which is
correct rather than a conflict: that label is scoring vocabulary and a
rationale is not scoring. `perjury` and `perjured` are legal conclusions
rather than intent words — they are on the list for the same underlying
reason, that a rationale is not the place to reach one, which is why the
opening sentence says intent OR a conclusion about conduct.
It is a data file rather than a Python constant on purpose, and for the
same two reasons `eval/weights.json` is: a frozen list can carry its own
written rationale, and widening it should be a visible diff in data rather
than an edit buried in code. There is a third reason here. Rule 2 holds the
deception vocabulary to live only inside `backend/app/referee/`, which is
scoring, and `test_eval.py` asserts it. This file defines those words for
the opposite purpose: so that nothing can publish them. No module outside
the referee holds the vocabulary, and the runtime guard is still real.
That guard scans every shipped code and data file, not only Python, and
names this file and `backend/app/referee/` as its only two exceptions. A
second JSON carrying these words would fail it.
`lie` and `lies` are on the list knowing that English also uses them for
where a room sits on a floor plan, or where responsibility rests. A rare
false refusal costs one turn and asks the model to restate; letting the
word through costs the rule. Both are also in the invariant above, so
leaving them off here would have the guard permit what the invariant
forbids.
Matching is case-insensitive and on word boundaries, so `believe` is not
caught by its first three letters.
